analysis.one_liner: Charges cargo ships fees for their air pollution and spends the money cleaning up U.S. ports.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge large cargo ships a fee for every ton of fuel they burn on voyages delivering goods to U.S. ports — $150 per ton of carbon dioxide-equivalent, plus fees for nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and fine particulate matter that worsen air quality. It would also charge importers whose goods travel through foreign ports on the way to the U.S., and it would spend the revenue on cleaner ships, electric ferries and harbor craft, port air monitoring, and workforce training. Ships or importers that refused to pay would be barred from U.S. ports or have their cargo seized.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near ports, which the bill's findings say suffer worse health outcomes from port air pollution, would benefit from lower ship emissions and new fenceline air monitoring within a mile of port boundaries. The climate benefits from reduced shipping emissions, which the bill says account for nearly 3 percent of global carbon dioxide output. U.S. maritime workers would gain training programs, and owners of Jones Act vessels, ferry operators, and harbor craft owners would gain grants, rebates, and low-interest loans to go electric or switch to low-carbon fuels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Port-neighborhood residents and U.S. maritime workers

how_it_helps.text: It puts a price on the pollution from large cargo ships — $150 per metric ton of carbon dioxide-equivalent, plus per-pound fees on nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, and fine particulate matter — with the rates rising each year by inflation plus 5 percentage points, so shipping companies have a growing financial reason to clean up their fuel.

It gives port-adjacent communities new tools: 3 percent of the fee revenue would fund fenceline air monitoring at port boundaries and in neighborhoods within one mile of a port, directly addressing the bill's finding that ports worsen health outcomes for nearby residents.

It recycles roughly half the fee revenue into U.S. ports and vessels: grants to replace or retrofit Jones Act ships, competitive grants for low-carbon maritime fuels, electrification of harbor craft and ferries, workforce training at maritime academies, and funding for existing clean ports and port infrastructure programs.

It has real teeth: the Coast Guard can prohibit a shipping operator that does not pay its fees from operating in U.S. waters or docking at U.S. ports, and Customs and Border Protection must seize the cargo of importers who cannot prove they paid.

It closes the loophole of routing cargo through foreign ports by charging importers a prorated fee on goods offloaded abroad that are ultimately bound for the United States, and it reduces the fee for ships already paying a comparable pollution fee in another country.

analysis.who_pays: International ocean shipping companies would pay the fees on every ton of fuel burned on voyages to U.S. ports, with fuel burned in polar regions charged at triple the rate. Importers would pay prorated fees on cargo shipped through foreign ports for eventual U.S. delivery, and both would face compliance costs from extensive per-voyage fuel and cargo reporting. Those costs would ultimately be passed into the prices of imported goods, so consumers would pay somewhat more for shipped products.

drawbacks.text: The fees would raise the cost of moving goods, and shipping lines and importers would pass much of that into retail prices, so ordinary consumers would pay somewhat more for imported goods even while benefiting from cleaner air.

The compliance burden is heavy: every covered voyage must report origin, distance, fuel consumed by type, cargo mass, intermediate ports, time on shore power, and more, each quarter, which is a substantial administrative cost for operators and importers.

The $150 per ton carbon price is far above most existing carbon prices worldwide, and the partial credit for foreign pollution fees could create trade friction with countries that price carbon at lower levels, since the U.S. fee would still apply on top of theirs.

A quarter of the revenue would go to owners of Jones Act vessels — a protected domestic fleet that already benefits from a legal monopoly on domestic shipping — which entrenches an existing concentrated interest as a beneficiary of a public-purpose fee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health and climate case is real: shipping is a large and fast-growing source of carbon emissions, and port pollution measurably harms nearby neighborhoods. The main cost is higher prices on imported goods and significant compliance paperwork, which is the unavoidable trade-off of any pollution fee. The design is fairly strong — enforcement via port bans and cargo seizures, recognition of foreign fees, and a sunset if the International Maritime Organization imposes an equivalent global fee — but the generous carve-out for the protected Jones Act fleet weakens the claim that this is purely a public-interest measure. On balance the benefits to port communities and the climate would plausibly outweigh the modest price increases for consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and the bill died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on June 8, 2023, with Senators Padilla and Welch, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
Four Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill sat in committee for the remaining eighteen months of the Congress.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: International shipping operators and importers are better off, because they continue to pay nothing for the emissions from voyages to U.S. ports. Port-neighborhood residents and U.S. maritime workers, who would have gained cleaner air, monitoring, and training programs, got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Shipping lines and importers kept paying nothing

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call showing how the chambers would have split.

industries.industry: International ocean shipping and container lines
industries.note: The bill would charge these companies per ton of fuel burned on U.S.-bound voyages and could bar nonpaying operators from U.S. ports. Their interest in avoiding the fee runs against the public's interest in cleaner air, since their emissions are what the fee exists to reduce.

industries.industry: Importers and retailers dependent on container shipping
industries.note: Importers would pay prorated fees on cargo routed through foreign ports, plus new reporting duties, with cargo seized for nonpayment. The industry's interest in avoiding the fee conflicts with the air-quality benefit, though some of the cost would land on consumers.

industries.industry: U.S. Jones Act fleet owners and domestic shipbuilders
industries.note: A quarter of the fee revenue would fund grants, rebates, and low-interest loans to replace or retrofit Jones Act vessels with battery or low-carbon propulsion, entrenching this legally protected fleet as a permanent beneficiary of the program.
Ports would receive funding for clean ports programs, infrastructure development, port air monitoring, and electrification of port equipment, funded entirely by the shipping fees.

industries.industry: Ferry, harbor craft, and sustainable-fuel producers
industries.note: About 45 percent of revenue would flow to electrifying ferries and harbor craft, low-carbon maritime fuel R&D, and workforce training — a new funding stream for companies and research institutions in those fields.
